title: Why does the Moon always show the same face?
hook: It does spin. Just in perfect step with its orbit.
summary: The Moon takes as long to spin once as it does to orbit Earth, so the same side always faces us.
cardText: It does spin, but one turn takes as long as one orbit of Earth: about 27 days. So the same face always points our way.

cardBlocks.text: Look at the full Moon tonight and again in ten years: you will see the same dark patches. That does not mean the Moon stays still. It does rotate, but one spin takes exactly as long as one trip around Earth: about 27 days.

So the same face always points our way. Astronomers call this synchronous rotation, or tidal locking. Early in its history the Moon spun faster. Earth’s gravity stretched it slightly out of round, and that bulge acted like a brake until the two rhythms matched.
The Moon does spin, but each turn lasts exactly one orbit.

deepDiveBlocks.text: The far side is not dark
The side we never see is not always dark: it gets sunlight too, and simply never points at Earth. At new Moon, when the near side is in shadow, the far side is in full daylight.

A slight rocking and wobbling of the Moon as seen from Earth, called libration, lets us see up to 59% of its surface over time, a little more than half. The first photo of the far side was taken by the Soviet probe Luna 3 in 1959.
Tidal locking is common in the Solar System: Jupiter’s four large moons also keep one face turned toward their planet.

claims.text: The far side of the Moon also gets sunlight; it is not permanently dark and simply never faces Earth.

support.excerpt: Some people call the far side – the hemisphere we never see from Earth – the "dark side", but that's misleading. As the Moon orbits Earth, different parts are in sunlight or darkness at different times.

claims.text: At new Moon, the far side is in full sunlight while the near side is dark.

support.excerpt: And a "new moon" occurs when the far side of the Moon has full sunlight, and the side facing us is having its night.

support.excerpt: Over time, it’s possible to see as much as 59% of the moon’s surface, due to a combination of motions – in particular, a slight north-south rocking and east-west wobbling of the moon – known as lunar libration.
